t: Create Target Array in the Given Order — Editorial
o: We simulate building an array where each value `nums[i]` is inserted at position `index[i]`, shifting existing elements right if needed. In Example 1, inserting 3 at index 2 turns `[0,1,2]` into `[0,1,3,2]`, and later inserting 4 at index 1 yields `[0,4,1,3,2]`. Example 2 shows that inserting at index 0 pushes everything else right. Since `index[i] <= i` and lengths are at most 100, even a naive shift-per-insert simulation is trivially fast — no clever data structure is required.
k: The problem is a direct simulation: each insertion at index k shifts all elements from k onward one position to the right.
Because n <= 100, an O(n^2) shifting approach is perfectly acceptable; no advanced structure is needed.
The guarantee index[i] <= i ensures every insertion index is valid for the current array size.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct Simulation with Insert (Brute Force)
a.i: Maintain a dynamic list and use the language's built-in insert operation, which shifts elements automatically. This mirrors the problem statement exactly and works because constraints are tiny.
s: For each i from 0 to n-1, insert nums[i] into target at position index[i].
a.t: O(n^2) — each of the n inserts may shift up to O(n) elements.
a.sp: O(n) — space for the output array (O(1) extra beyond it).

a.n: Approach 2: Shift Simulation with Manual Array (No Built-in Insert)
a.i: If built-in insert is disallowed (e.g., a follow-up), simulate manually: keep a size counter, shift elements from the end down to the insertion point one step right, then place the new value. This shows you understand what insert does under the hood.
s: Allocate an array target of length n and set size = 0.
For each i, shift target[size-1..index[i]] one position right.
Place nums[i] at target[index[i]] and increment size.
a.t: O(n^2) — worst case every insertion happens at index 0, shifting all prior elements.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the output array.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 since built-in insert/splice directly models the problem; mention Approach 2 to show you can implement the shifting yourself if asked. Common pitfalls: forgetting that inserting shifts existing elements right (not overwriting them), off-by-one errors in manual shift loops (shift from the end backward), and returning a fixed-size array with stale zeros instead of only `size` filled entries. Edge cases: single element, all insertions at index 0. Likely follow-ups: do it without built-in insert (Approach 2), or handle large n efficiently — which would require a balanced BST / order-statistic tree or offline processing with a BIT to achieve O(n log n).
